items.cleanReaderHtml:
recently completed a Master of Divinity postgraduate degree at Harvard Divinity School, focusing on comparative religion and sacred landscapes. She is originally from Bangor, Maine.

In October 1948, in Country Kerry, Ireland, Seán Ó Muircheartaigh met with Seosamh Ó Dálaigh to tell him about the woman who came from the sea. She had appeared, said Ó Muircheartaigh, one night on the magharees, those bright spits of sand that occasionally pop up amid the rain-lashed rocks of the Dingle peninsula. Alone on the beach, she settled herself on a rock and began combing her hair.

Also on the beach was a farmer, who – much to the surprise of the woman herself – would by daybreak become her husband. He’d come to gather seaweed, seeing her before she saw him. Beautiful as she was, the woman was also strange: the creature he saw stagger onto that Dingle beach was not a woman at all. It was a seal.

By the time Ó Muircheartaigh told Ó Dálaigh about the seal woman, he was already 80. He had been born in the apocalyptic aftermath of the Great Hunger that divested as much as a third of Ireland’s population to death or migration, and he had survived two great wars. Most of the disappeared were – like Ó Muircheartaigh himself – small farmers and native Irish, or Gaeilge, speakers. The famine had been not just a physical genocide: it had been a linguistic and cultural one, too.

Both Ó Muircheartaigh and Ó Dálaigh were veteran contributors to the Irish Folklore Commission: the former as a renowned storyteller; the latter, an equally renowned collector. The IFC is now the National Folklore Collection at University College Dublin ­– a behemoth of 3 million pages of texts and recordings. But in 1948, following eight centuries of colonialism, the loss of 99 per cent of the island’s forests, a staggering emigration , and the decline of the Irish language, the IFC was in a race against time and the fragility of memory. As it turned out, an awful lot of people had heard stories about seals that came to land as humans.

N owadays, these shapeshifters are known as ‘selkies’. Selkie is a Scots term that came into widespread use via a Joan Baez cover, ‘Silkie’ (1961), of a traditional Scottish folk song. Yet the phenomenon it describes – of creatures who shapeshift between human and seal forms by shedding a skin – appears consistently in folklore spanning the Celtic world and beyond, even as far as Sweden. Before Baez insinuated the term into international parlance, selkies were identified in Irish and English by a constellation of descriptors. In Irish, the most common is mhaighdean mhara , or ‘sea maiden’, referring to selkies and mermaids. Even in English, many storytellers use ‘mermaid’ for both the phocine and the piscine. Sometimes the two are differentiated with context (fish tails, seal skins), but what matters more than phenotyping is that the mermaid or selkie is neither quite human nor animal. What defines the selkie is transformation.

Much of the folklore retains the quality of the best gossip, hyper-local and yet vague. Storytellers name names, offer precise locations for key scenes in the story. And several admit something startling: that they themselves are the descendants of human-seal pairings.

After the farmer spotted the woman on the beach, Ó Muircheartaigh said, he saw something else. A sealskin cloak lay beside her: her ticket to transformation and a return to the sea. Then he made a choice that would ricochet throughout the generations, and leave the selkie with no option but to follow him home. He stole the selkie’s cloak and secreted it away, thus securing her for a bride. These rough beginnings aside, the couple produced a brood of children and went about the gruelling lives of any impoverished Irish fishing family. The only thing disrupting the fantasy of a normal human wife, acquired in normal human ways, was the webbing between the children’s toes. That, and the fact that the woman never smiled, but kept looking out towards the sea.

W hat does it mean if your grandmother was a seal? The folklore attests that marriages between humans and selkies were common enough to generate a host of human-selkie lineages – Conneely, Gallagher, Dowd, O’Kane, O’Shea, MacDuffie, McPhee, Flaherty, Glavin – whose members were predisposed towards webbed digits and an ineffable longing for the sea. (‘My mother was one of them O’Sheas,’ the railway worker Séamas MacMathghamhna confided to a folklore collector in 1949, after explaining the selkie lineage of the O’Sheas.) The Celtic studies scholar Gregory Darwin has identified nearly 50 family groups whose members carry selkie blood.

Now is a good time to have a seal in the family tree. As our planet hurtles through climate catastrophe, everyone from environmental activists and TikTok influencers to academics and New Age pilgrims is turning towards animals-as-family rhetoric. Such gusto stems from a cultural exhaustion with extractionism and with narratives of domination and human exceptionalism that have dogged the culture and geopolitics of the Global North since the 19th century. Yet the naivety with which the zeitgeist tends to approach an expanded view of interspecies kinship presents its own problems. For one, it doesn’t quite ring true – and it is hard to fight for a worldview that you can’t see clearly. For another, if we reframe our relationship with the more-than-human around intimate familial connection, then we need ways of understanding what happens when that connection becomes fraught.

The selkie story is one of family dysfunction par excellence. After all, the gutting truth at the centre of selkie families is that one’s origins lie in theft, violence, rape and unimaginable loss. The children of human-selkie pairings face a mottled inheritance, at best. Writing for The New York Times in 2008, Bryan Patrick Miller recounted how his great-great-great-grandfather’s kidnapping of a mhaighdean mhara cursed the family, causing the couple’s half-human children to flee across the Atlantic. Some coastal communities saw seals as fallen angels or the souls of drowned fishermen: mating with them was dubious to say the least.

Mottled or not, a selkie genealogy had to be reckoned with. Having a selkie in the family forced an acknowledgement of a mixed inheritance that was dark and disturbing, and in which successive generations continued to be implicated. Only by considering these uncomfortable reverberations of what it means to be family do we move closer to reimagining our relationships with the more-than-human world.

A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is an absolute dynamo in bed

Among folklorists, the trope of the selkie is generally known as the Seal Wife – a designation that speaks more to the gendered hold that the selkie story has on our imagination than to the actual folklore topos. The selkie’s allure is such that men will risk curses and commit theft and kidnapping to possess her, regardless of the certain tragedy that forced marriage augurs. Yet the selkies of folklore are not necessarily wives, women or even seals (note the mermaids, above). Male selkies occasionally make cameos as the kidnapped selkie wife’s jilted husband, father of her aquatic children, keening for her release from outside the human husband’s house. At other times, they appear as her brother, or as characters in the quotidian interactions between humans and their environment: they are accidentally killed, kidnapped as pets, steal fish, issue prophesies, plead and bargain, proffer advice and opinions.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A pesar de la escasa visibilidad que suele caracterizar a las aguas costeras del Atlántico sudoccidental en Uruguay, el empleo de nuevas metodologías de filmación submarina ha permitido obtener los primeros registros en video de alta calidad sobre la fauna de condrictios en la costa rochense. El Dr. Andrés Milessi (Biólogo marino) y el investigador Agustín Loureiro, integrantes de la Iniciativa Mar Azul Uruguayo, presentaron en SobreCiencia los resultados de la campaña de monitoreo llevada a cabo en el entorno de La Paloma (Rocha).

Loureiro explicó que el equipo desarrolló dispositivos de video remoto subacuático con carnada (BRUV, por sus siglas en inglés) fabricados con estructuras livianas de termofusión y cámaras calibradas para operar en condiciones de turbidez. Las filmaciones confirmaron la presencia del Tiburón Pintarroja (Schroederichthys saurisqualus), una especie costera que utiliza las aguas uruguayas como zona de parición y cría. Paralelamente, los científicos recopilaron datos mediante marcaje satelital coordinado con investigadores de San Clemente del Tuyú (Argentina) para seguir las rutas migratorias de los ejemplares, registrando además especímenes amenazados de pez guitarra chica (Zapteryx brevirostris) y diversos tipos de rayas en actividades de buceo libre. Ante este escenario, Milessi enfatizó que no existen registros de ataques ni riesgo para los bañistas, e hizo un llamado a trabajar junto a la Dirección Nacional de Recursos Acuáticos (Dinara) y el Ministerio de Ambiente para implementar protocolos de devolución obligatoria en la pesca recreativa y avanzar en la delimitación de nuevas Áreas Marinas Protegidas.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
El consumo de yerba mate (Ilex paraguariensis) constituye una de las prácticas culturales y alimentarias más extendidas en Uruguay, registrándose importantes líneas de investigación sobre sus propiedades nutricionales e industriales. La Dra. Andrea Cano, investigadora del Departamento de Ciencia y Tecnología de los Alimentos de la Facultad de Química (Universidad de la República), abordó los aspectos bioquímicos que caracterizan a esta infusión y los efectos de su procesamiento en el perfil sensorial.

Cano aclaró que el término «mateína» es una denominación popular en desuso, dado que la molécula responsable del estímulo nervioso es exactamente la cafeína. No obstante, la investigadora precisó que, a diferencia del café espresso, el mate libera la cafeína de manera gradual durante las sucesivas cebadas, evitando picos repentinos de energía y reduciendo progresivamente la fatiga. Asimismo, la especialista resaltó la alta concentración de polifenoles (compuestos antioxidantes que inhiben la oxidación celular) y la presencia de saponinas, sustancias tensoactivas responsables del amargor inicial y de la formación de la espuma en la superficie. Finalmente, Cano detalló que la yerba consumida en Uruguay atraviesa un periodo de estacionamiento prolongado de varios meses que transforma la clorofila en feofitinas —otorgándole su tonalidad verde oliva y su amargor característico— y repasó su experiencia como jurado técnico en el primer Mundial de la Yerba Mate celebrado en Buenos Aires.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age.”

Long before there was Yo-Yo Ma, there was Spanish Catalan cellist and conductor Pablo Casals (December 29, 1876–October 22, 1973), regarded by many — including Yo-Yo Ma — as the greatest cellist of all time. The recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the U.N. Peace Medal for his unflinching dedication to justice and his lifelong stance against oppression and dictatorship, Casals was as much an extraordinary artist as he was an extraordinary human being — a generous and kind man of uncommon compassion and goodness of heart, a passionate spirit in love with life, and an unflinching idealist.

And yet, like many exceptional people, he cultivated his character through an early brush with suffering. In his late teenage years, already a celebrated prodigy, he underwent an anguishing spiritual crisis of the kind Tolstoy faced in his later years and came close to suicide. But with the loving support of his mother, he regained his center and went on to become a man of great talent, great accomplishment, and great vitality.

To mark his ninetieth birthday, Casals began a collaboration with photojournalist Albert E. Kahn that would eventually become the 1970 autobiography-of-sorts Joys and Sorrows (public library) — one of the most magnificent perspectives of the creative life ever committed to words.

Straight from the opening, Casals cracks open the essence of his extraordinary character and the source of his exuberant life-energy with a beautiful case for how purposeful work is the true fountain of youth:

On my last birthday I was ninety-three years old. That is not young, of course. In fact, it is older than ninety. But age is a relative matter. If you continue to work and to absorb the beauty in the world about you, you find that age does not necessarily mean getting old. At least, not in the ordinary sense. I feel many things more intensely than ever before, and for me life grows more fascinating.

Recounting being at once delighted and unsurprised by an article in the London Sunday Times about an orchestra in the Caucasus composed of musicians older than a hundred, he considers the spring of their vitality:

In spite of their age, those musicians have not lost their zest for life. How does one explain this? I do not think the answer lies simply in their physical constitutions or in something unique about the climate in which they live. It has to do with their attitude toward life; and I believe that their ability to work is due in no small measure to the fact that they do work. Work helps prevent one from getting old. I, for one, cannot dream of retiring. Not now or ever. Retire? The word is alien and the idea inconceivable to me. I don’t believe in retirement for anyone in my type of work, not while the spirit remains. My work is my life. I cannot think of one without the other. To “retire” means to me to begin to die. The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age. Each day I am reborn. Each day I must begin again.

For the past eighty years I have started each day in the same manner.

With great elegance, he contrasts the dullness of mindless routine with the exhilaration of mindful ritual — something many great artists engineer into their days. In a sentiment Henry Miller would come to echo only two years later in his own memorable meditation on the secret of remaining forever young, Casals writes of his daily practice:

It is not a mechanical routine but something essential to my daily life. I go to the piano, and I play two preludes and fugues of Bach. I cannot think of doing otherwise. It is a sort of benediction on the house. But that is not its only meaning for me. It is a rediscovery of the world of which I have the joy of being a part. It fills me with awareness of the wonder of life, with a feeling of the incredible marvel of being a human being. The music is never the same for me, never. Each day is something new, fantastic, unbelievable. That is Bach, like nature, a miracle!

Casals, indeed, finds great vitalization in bearing witness to nature’s mastery of the self-renewal so essential for the human spirit over the long run:

I do not think a day passes in my life in which I fail to look with fresh amazement at the miracle of nature. It is there on every side. It can be simply a shadow on a mountainside, or a spider’s web gleaming with dew, or sunlight on the leaves of a tree. I have always especially loved the sea. Whenever possible, I have lived by the sea… It has long been a custom of mine to walk along the beach each morning before I start to work. True, my walks are shorter than they used to be, but that does not lessen the wonder of the sea. How mysterious and beautiful is the sea! how infinitely variable! It is never the same, never, not from one moment to the next, always in the process of change, always becoming something different and new.

In the same way, Casals argues, we renew ourselves through purposeful work. But he adds an admonition about the complacency of talent, echoing Jack Kerouac’s fantastic distinction between talent and genius. Casals offers aspiring artists of all stripes a word of advice on humility and hard work as the surest path to self-actualization:

I see no particular merit in the fact that I was an artist at the age of eleven. I was born with an ability, with music in me, that is all. No special credit was due me. The only credit we can claim is for the use we make of the talent we are given. That is why I urge young musicians: “Don’t be vain because you happen to have talent. You are not responsible for that; it was not of your doing. What you do with your talent is what matters. You must cherish this gift. Do not demean or waste what you have been given. Work — work constantly and nourish it.”

Of course the gift to be cherished most of all is that of life itself. One’s work should be a salute to life.

Hence Ray Bradbury’s famous proclamation that he never worked a day in his life — further testament to the magic made possible by discerning your vocation.

Casals lived and worked for another four years, dying eight weeks before his ninety-seventh birthday. Joys and Sorrows remains an invigorating read — a rare glimpse into the source of this creative and spiritual vitality of unparalleled proportions.

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
La consolidación de la industria forestal en Uruguay —que genera cerca de 20.000 puestos de trabajo y abarca más de un 95% de bosques certificados bajo estándares de sostenibilidad— impulsó la creación de capacidades académicas descentralizadas en el territorio nacional. El Ing. Agr. Diego Pasarella, coordinador de la carrera de Ingeniería Forestal en la Facultad de Agronomía (Universidad de la República), expuso los pilares académicos de esta titulación universitaria que se dicta 100% de forma presencial en la sede Tacuarembó de la Udelar desde el año 2014.

Pasarella destacó que la carrera integra fundamentos de física, matemática, biología y química con conocimientos agronómicos e ingeniería de procesos. Esta formación híbrida permite a los profesionales desempeñarse tanto en la gestión de campo y planificación del patrimonio forestal como en plantas industriales y laboratorios de control de calidad. El docente subrayó la alta tasa de inserción laboral de sus egresados y el rol de la ingeniería en la transformación mecánica de la madera uruguaya hacia productos de elevado valor agregado, citando como ejemplo los avances en arquitectura estructural masiva en madera para edificaciones y la sustitución de productos importados derivados de la deforestación de bosques tropicales.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Si bien los grandes dinosaurios concentran gran parte de la atención paleontológica, el registro fósil del norte y oeste del Uruguay atesora evidencias de otros grupos de reptiles arcosaurios que dominaron los ecosistemas mesozoicos hace más de 100 millones de años. En el cierre de la serie especial La era de los dinosaurios, el Lic. Matías Soto, geólogo y paleontólogo de la Facultad de Ciencias (Universidad de la República), detalló los avances en la identificación de pterosaurios y cocodrilos prehistóricos hallados en los departamentos de Tacuarembó y Paysandú.

Soto explicó que los pterosaurios (reptiles voladores provistos de una membrana alar sostenida por el cuarto dedo de la mano) están representados en el país por fragmentos de hocico y dientes alargados colectados en Tacuarembó (Tacuadactylus luciae). En cuanto a los cocodrilos del Mesozoico, el investigador destacó la coexistencia de formas con morfologías y dietas sumamente heterogéneas: por un lado, el Meridiosaurus vallisparadisi (descubierto en Valle Edén, Tacuarembó), un espécimen de hábitos acuáticos y hocico estrecho similar al gavial del Ganges especializado en la captura de peces; y por otro lado, el Uruguaysuchus aznarezi (hallado en Guichón, Paysandú), un cocodrilo netamente terrestre de 1,20 metros de longitud, postura erguida y narinas frontales. El especialista remarcó que los laboratorios de la Facultad de Ciencias albergan más de un centenar de dientes de carnívoros, cientos de huesos de saurópodos (como Udelartitán) y materiales pendientes de estudio que permitirán describir nuevas especies para la paleontología nacional.

El instrument

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Con el objetivo de consolidar las capacidades científicas y promover la inserción de investigadores de alto nivel en el sistema productivo e institucional del país, la Agencia Nacional de Investigación e Innovación (ANII) mantiene abierta la recepción de propuestas para las Becas de Posdoctorado Nacional. El instrumento está dirigido a grupos de investigación pertenecientes a instituciones nacionales públicas o privadas sin fines de lucro que incorporen a un doctor o doctora para el desarrollo de proyectos de investigación aplicada.

Las becas otorgan un financiamiento de hasta 24 meses, cubriendo el 80% del estipendio mensual ($ 90.000 uruguayos proporcionados por ANII), mientras que la institución beneficiaria aporta el 20% restante. Adicionalmente, el programa otorga un fondo único de $ 90.000 para gastos de movilidad e insumos de laboratorio. En esta edición, las propuestas deben alinearse a tres de los seis ejes priorizados en el borrador del Plan Estratégico Nacional de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación (PENCTI): Trabajo y producción / Crecimiento y desarrollo, Seguridad ciudadana e integral, y Desigualdad social, de género y territorial. Las inscripciones permanecen abiertas hasta el 1° de diciembre en la plataforma web institucional (www.anii.org.uy).

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising.

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson—the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.

For quilter Rosy Petri, Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery.

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network (WCQN), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix—in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”

We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release, Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers.

items.title: The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype
items.author: Thomas Macaulay
items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body…

videos.caption: Enlace audiovisual citado en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive.

What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.

The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.

Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry.

The AI Hype Index returns

Separating AI reality from hyped-up fiction isn’t always easy. That’s why we’ve created the AI Hype Index—a simple, at-a-glance summary of what’s shaping the industry right now.

The latest edition tracks AI’s spread across everything from literary prizes and cyberattacks to a Grok-ified version of The Odyssey. See where it all landed on this month’s index.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO
It eclipsed SpaceX as the largest stock-market debut. (Bloomberg $)
+ Its stated mission could conflict with shareholders’ interests. (NYT $)
+ The IPO comes amid new safety fears about its AI advances. (FT $)
+ Its performance will test the strength of the AI boom. (BBC)
+ What even is the AI bubble? (MIT Technology Review)

2 China is reportedly seeking Nvidia chips for AI-powered weapons
Beijing is trying to circumvent US export controls. (CNBC)
+ Alibaba tapped Nvidia to support a military-linked lab. (NYT $)
+ When the US military implemented AI, civilian deaths rose. (Intercept)
+ “Humans in the loop” in AI war is an illusion. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Elon Musk has joined Silicon Valley’s retreat from Trump
He called his midterm spending “foolish” and broke with MAGA. (FT $)
+ OpenAI and Palantir leaders have also struck new tones. (Gizmodo)
+ Silicon Valley got the midterms badly wrong. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Ukraine used relay drones to strike Putin’s bridge without Starlink
The strike showed how it’s learning to fight without SpaceX. (Ars Technica)
+ Musk has denied Kyiv’s claims about restrictions on Starlink. (CNBC)

5 A major cyberattack has hit the European Commission
It may have exposed large amounts of staff personal data. (Politico)
+ Trump has blamed Minnesota for water system hacks. (ABC)

6 Trump may force US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI
The proposal aims to discourage reliance on Chinese models. (Reuters $)

7 The US has slashed funding for biomedical science abroad
It’s also weakened oversight of foreign grants. (Economist $)

8 AI datacentres are set to drive a 70% rise in emissions by 2030
The US and China are turning to fossil fuels to power AI. (Guardian)
+ The climate case for AI has not been made. (MIT Technology Review)

9 Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the best-reviewed game ever
It scored 99 out of 100 on review aggregation site Metacritic. (BBC)
+ Schools and businesses are bracing for “GTA Flu” season. (NYT $)

10 A new underwater research station aims to protect coral reefs
Aquanauts there will monitor struggling ecosystems. (New Scientist $)

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic.”

—Thomas Nagel, a philosopher and professor emeritus at NYU, tells Wired why he objects to Anthropic giving Claude more independence, just as the company makes its record-breaking stock-market debut.


China has approved the world’s first invasive brain-computer chip—here’s what’s next

Sitting in the courtyard of his house in China’s Henan province last October, Dong Hui decided to try holding a pen. Six years after a car accident left him paralyzed from the neck down, he slowly wrote his name, “Thank you,” and the date.

items.author: Maria Popova

The Marginalian

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“In disputes upon moral or scientific points, ever let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.”

Manners today are often seen as a quaint subject that belongs in Lord Chesterfield’s outlandish advice on the art of pleasing or Esquire‘s dated guide to dating. But in a culture where we regularly do online what we’d never do in person and behave offline in ways our grandparents wouldn’t have dared dream of even in their most defiant fantasies, there’s something to be said for the lost art of, if not “manners,” politeness and simple respect in communication. Though originally published in 1866, Martine’s Hand-book of Etiquette, and Guide to True Politeness (public library; public domain; free Kindle download) by Arthur Martine contains a treasure trove of timeless — and increasingly timely — pointers on the necessary art of living up to our social-animal destiny.

Martine contextualizes his mission:

Politeness has been defined as an “artificial good-nature;” but it would be better said that good-nature is natural politeness. It inspires us with an unremitting attention, both to please others and to avoid giving them offense. Its code is a ceremonial, agreed upon and established among mankind, to give each other external testimonies of friendship or respect. Politeness and etiquette form a sort of supplement to the law, which enables society to protect itself against offenses which the law cannot touch. For instance, the law cannot punish a man for habitually staring at people in an insolent and annoying manner, but etiquette can banish such an offender from the circles of good society, and fix upon him the brand of vulgarity. Etiquette consists in certain forms, ceremonies, and rules which the principle of politeness establishes and enforces for the regulation of the manners of men and women in their intercourse with each other.

[…]

The true aim of politeness, is to make those with whom you associate as well satisfied with themselves as possible. … Politeness is a sort of social benevolence, which avoids wounding the pride, or shocking the prejudices of those around you.

But he offers an important disclaimer:

[Politeness] must be cultivated, for the promptings of nature are eminently selfish, and courtesy and good-breeding are only attainable by effort and discipline. But even courtesy has limits where dignity should govern it, for when carried to excess, particularly in manner, it borders on sycophancy, which is almost as despicable as rudeness. To overburden people with attention; to render them uncomfortable with a prodigality of proffered services; to insist upon obligations which they do not desire, is not only to render yourself disagreeable, but contemptible.

Among Martine’s most timeless advice are his guidelines on the art of conversation, to which an entire section of the book is dedicated. He begins:

As the object of conversation is pleasure and improvement, those subjects only which are of universal interest can be made legitimate topics of pleasantry or discussion. And it is the gift of expressing thoughts and fancies in a quick, brilliant, and graceful manner on such topics,—of striking out new ideas, eliciting the views and opinions of others, of attaching the interest of all to the subject discussed, giving it, however trifling in itself, weight and importance in the estimation of the hearers, that constitutes the great talent for conversation. But this talent can never, we may safely aver, be displayed except in a good cause, and when conversation is carried on in a spirit of genuine charity and benevolence.

He offers a few pointers:

  1. Know when not to speak:

    2. The power of preserving silence is the very first requisite to all who wish to shine, or even please in discourse; and those who cannot preserve it, have really no business to speak. … The silence that, without any deferential air, listens with polite attention, is more flattering than compliments, and more frequently broken for the purpose of encouraging others to speak, than to display the listener’s own powers. This is the really eloquent silence. It requires great genius—more perhaps than speaking—and few are gifted with the talent…

  2. Mind the rudeness of laconic response:

    3. Never give short or sharp answers in ordinary conversation, unless you aspire to gain distinction by mere rudeness; for they have in fact no merit, and are only uncivil. “I do not know,” “I cannot tell,” are the most harmless words possible, and may yet be rendered very offensive by the tone and manner in which they are pronounced. Never reply, in answer to a question like the following, “Did Mrs. Spitewell tell you how Miss Rosebud’s marriage was getting on?” “I did not ask.” It is almost like saying, I never ask impertinent questions, though you do; we learn plenty of things in the world without having first inquired about them. If you must say, you did not ask, say, that “you forgot to ask,” “neglected it,” or “did not think of it.” We can always be ordinarily civil, even if we cannot always be absolutely wise.

  3. Don’t be a self-righteous contrarian:

    4. Leave quibbling of every kind to lawyers pleading at the bar for the life of a culprit; in society and conversation it is invariably out of place, unless when Laughter is going his merry round. At all other times it is a proof of bad breeding.

He then goes on to outline a cautionary taxonomy of “bores” and other ill-mannered conversation archetypes, diagnosing the specific downfall of each:

  1. The loud talker, who “silences a whole party by his sole power of lungs”:

    2. All subjects are alike to him; he speaks on every topic with equal fluency, is never at a loss, quotes high authority for every assertion, and allows no one else to utter a word; he silences, without the least ceremony, every attempt at interruption, however cleverly managed. … Great, and especially loud and positive talkers, have been denounced by all writers on manners as shallow and superficial persons.

  2. The excessive life-sharer, whom you no doubt know well from your Facebook timeline:

    3. [This is] the man who gives an account of his dogs, horses, lands, books, and pictures. Whatever is his, must, he thinks, interest others; and listen they must, however resolutely they may attempt to change the current of his discourse.

    Women of this class are sometimes too fond of praising their children. It is no doubt an amiable weakness; but I would still advise them to indulge as little as possible in the practice; for however dear the rosy-cheeked, curly-headed prattlers may be to them, the chances are, that others will vote the darlings to be great bores; you that have children, never speak of them in company.

  3. The clever bore “takes up every idle speech, to show his wisdom at a cheap rate”:

    4. The grave expounder of truisms belongs to this class. He cannot allow the simplest conversation to go on, without entering into proofs and details familiar to every child nine years of age; and the tenor of his discourse, however courteous in terms and manner, pays you the very indifferent compliment, of supposing that you have fallen from some other planet, in total and absolute ignorance of the most ordinary and every-day things connected with this little world of ours. All foreigners are particularly great at this style of boring.

  4. The indifferent or apathetic bore parades his inattentiveness in your face:

    5. If he refrains from the direct and absolute rudeness of yawning in your face, [he] shows, by short and drawling answers, given at fits and starts, and completely at variance with the object of the conversation, that he affects at least a total indifference to the party present, and to the subject of discourse. In society, the absent man is uncivil; he who affects to be so, is rude and vulgar. All persons who speak of their ailings, diseases, or bodily infirmities, are offensive bores. Subjects of this sort should be addressed to doctors, who are paid for listening to them, and to no one else. Bad taste is the failing of these bores.

  5. The lingering bore who overstays his welcome:

    6. [These are] the ladies and gentlemen who pay long visits, and who, meeting you at the door prepared to sally forth, keep you talking near the fire till the beauty of the day is passed; and then take their leave, “hoping they have not detained you.” Bad feeling or want of tact here predominates.

  6. The hobby-riders, who sound like a broken record:

    7. [They] constantly speak on the same eternal subject [and] bore you at all times and at all hours, whether you are in health or in sickness, in spirits or in sorrow, with the same endless topic, must not be overlooked in our list; though it is sufficient to denounce them. Their failing is occasioned by a total want of judgment.

  7. The Malaprops, with their special gift for choosing the least appropriate topics of conversation:

    8. A numerous and unhappy family [who] are constantly addressing the most unsuitable speeches to individuals or parties. To the blind they will speak of fine pictures and scenery; and will entertain a person in deep mourning with the anticipated pleasures of to-morrow’s ball. A total want of ordinary thought and observation, is the general cause of the Malaprop failing.

  8. The egotistical bore, who stifles with his vanity:

    9. It is truly revolting, indeed, to approach the very Boa-constrictor of good society; the snake who comes upon us, not in the natural form of a huge, coarse, slow reptile, but Proteus-like, in a thousand different forms; though all displaying at the first sight the boa-bore, ready to slime over every subject of discourse with the vile saliva of selfish vanity. Pah! it is repulsive even to speak of the species, numerous, too, as the sands along the shore.

Martine adds an admonition against talking too much by way of Jonathan Swift, who observed:

Nothing is more generally exploded than the folly of talking too much; yet I rarely remember to have seen five people together, where some one among them hath not been predominant in that kind, to the great constraint and disgust of all the rest. But among such as deal in multitudes of words, none are comparable to the sober, deliberate talker, who proceedeth with much thought and caution, maketh his preface, brancheth out into several digressions, findeth a hint that putteth him in mind of another story, which he promises to tell you when this is done, cometh back regularly to his subject, cannot readily call to mind some person’s name, holdeth his head, complaineth of his memory; the whole company all this while in suspense; at last says, it is no matter, and so goes on. And to crown the business, it perhaps proveth at last a story the company has heard fifty times before, or at best some insipid adventure of the relater.

He then offers his own counsel on striking the right balance:

In conversation there must be, as in love and in war, some hazarding, some rattling on; nor need twenty falls affect you, so long as you take cheerfulness and good humor for your guides; but the careful and measured conversation just described is always, though perfectly correct, extremely dull and tedious — a vast blunder from first to last.

Martine quotes La Bruyère:

The great charm of conversation consists less in the display of one’s own wit and intelligence, than in the power to draw forth the resources of others; he who leaves you after a long conversation, pleased with himself and the part he has taken in the discourse, will be your warmest admirer. Men do not care to admire you, they wish you to be pleased with them; they do not seek for instruction or even amusement from your discourse, but they do wish you to be made acquainted with their talents and powers of conversation; and the true man of genius will delicately make all who come in contact with him feel the exquisite satisfaction of knowing that they have appeared to advantage.

Of the vanity of knowledge — which makes it tempting to learn to talk about books you haven’t read — Martine observes:

No, no, let us not deceive ourselves; we never want subjects of conversation; but we often want the knowledge how to treat them; above all, how to bring them forward in a graceful and pleasing manner.

He then recapitulates the essence of the art of conversation:

Cheerfulness, unaffected cheerfulness, a sincere desire to please and be pleased, unchecked by any efforts to shine, are the qualities you must bring with you into society, if you wish to succeed in conversation. … a light and airy equanimity of temper,—that spirit which never rises to boisterousness, and never sinks to immovable dullness; that moves gracefully from “grave to gay, from serious to serene,” and by mere manner gives proof of a feeling heart and generous mind.

The chapter ends with some “general rules for conversation,” in which Martine presents a selection of do’s and don’ts. Here is a synthesis of his most salient points:

  1. Don’t correct your conversation partner or go on righteousness crusades. It is a sign of, at best, vanity or, at worst, sheer rudeness to force your opinion on another.

    2. Reproof is a medicine like mercury or opium; if it be improperly administered, with report either to the adviser or the advised, it will do harm instead of good.

    If a man is telling that which is as old as the hills, or which you believe to be false, the better way is to let him go on. Why should you refuse a man the pleasure of believing that he is telling you something which you never heard before? Besides, by refusing to believe him, or by telling him that his story is old, you not only mortify him, but the whole company is made uneasy, and, by sympathy, share his mortification.

    It is bad manners to satirize lawyers in the presence of lawyers, or doctors in the presence of one of that calling, and so of all the professions. Nor should you rail against bribery and corruption in the presence of politicians, (especially of a New York politician,) or members of Congress, as they will have good reason to suppose that you are hinting at them. It is the aim of politeness to leave the arena of social intercourse untainted with any severity of language, or bitterness of feeling.

    Whenever the lady or gentleman with whom you are discussing a point, whether of love, war, science or politics, begins to sophisticate, drop the subject instantly. Your adversary either wants the ability to maintain his opinion,– and then it would be uncivil to press it — or he wants the still more useful ability to yield the point with unaffected grace and good-humor; or what is also possible, his vanity is in some way engaged in defending views on which he may probably have acted, so that to demolish his opinions is perhaps to reprove his conduct, and no well-bred man goes into society for the purpose of sermonizing.

    To reprove with success, the following circumstances are necessary, viz.: mildness, secrecy, intimacy, and the esteem of the person you would reprove.

  2. Be selective. Novelist William Gibson has stressed the importance of a “personal micro-culture”. Susan Sontag wrote in her diary that she’s only interested in people engaged in a project of self-transformation. Artist Austin Kleon has astutely argued that “you are a mashup of what you let into your life.” Martine suggests the same is true of selecting your conversation company:

    3. If you have been once in company with an idle person, it is enough. You need never go again. You have heard all he knows. And he has had no opportunity of learning anything new. For idle people make no improvements.

    Don’t give your time to every superficial acquaintance: it is bestowing what is to you of inestimable worth, upon one who is not likely to be the better for it.

  3. Keep your commitments but give those who fail to keep theirs the benefit of the doubt:

    4. Be careful of your word, even in keeping the most trifling appointment. But do not blame another for a failure of that kind, till you have heard his excuse.

  4. Be mindful of your audience and don’t parade your knowledge before those less learned:

    5. All local wits, all those whose jests are understood only within the range of their own circle or coterie, are decided objectionables in general society. It is the height of ill-breeding, in fact, to converse, or jest, on subjects that are not perfectly understood by the party at large; it is a species of rude mystification, as uncivil as whispering, or as speaking in language that may not be familiar to some of the party. But you must not make a fool of yourself, even if others show themselves deficient in good manners; and must not, like inflated simpletons, fancy yourself the object of every idle jest you do not understand, or of every laugh that chance may have called forth. Ladies and gentlemen feel that they are neither laughed at nor ridiculed.

    In society, the object of conversation is of course entertainment and improvement, and it must, therefore, be adapted to the circle in which it is carried on, and must be neither too high nor too deep for the party at large, so that every one may contribute his share, just at his pleasure, and to the best of his ability.

    A gentleman will, by all means, avoid showing his learning and accomplishments in the presence of ignorant and vulgar people, who can, by no possibility, understand or appreciate them. It is a pretty sure sign of bad breeding to set people to staring and feeling uncomfortable.

    In a mixed company, never speak to your friend of a matter which the rest do not understand, unless it is something which you can explain to them, and which may be made interesting to the whole party.

    Do not endeavor to shine in all companies. Leave room for your hearers to imagine something within you beyond all you have said.

    Think like the wise; but talk like ordinary people. Never go out of the common road, but for somewhat.

    Put yourself on the same level as the person to whom you speak, and under penalty of being considered a pedantic idiot, refrain from explaining any expression or word that you may use.

  5. Omission isn’t lying, it’s politeness. (Here we might disagree with Martine.) Learn to evade.

    6. You need not tell all the truth, unless to those who have a right to know it all. But let all you tell be truth.

  6. Say “yes” whenever possible. When you say “no,” do so firmly:

    7. If a favor is asked of you, grant it, if you can. If not, refuse it in such a manner, as that one denial may be sufficient.

  7. Let your opinion change — advice particularly apt in today’s hasty culture where not having an opinion is considered an embarrassment; seek to understand rather than to be right, and don’t be a know-it-all:

    8. Fools pretend to foretell what will be the issue of things, and are laughed at for their awkward conjectures. Wise men, being aware of the uncertainty of human affairs, and having observed how small a matter often produces a great change, are modest in their conjectures.

    Reflect upon the different appearances things make to you from what they did some years ago, and don’t imagine that your opinion will never alter, because you are extremely positive at present. Let the remembrance of your past changes of sentiment make you more flexible.

    In disputes upon moral or scientific points, ever let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.

    Give your opinion modestly, but freely; hear that of others with candor; and ever endeavor to find out, and to communicate truth.

    It is an advantage to have concealed one’s opinion. For by that means you may change your judgment of things (which every wise man finds reason to do) and not be accused of fickleness.

  8. Don’t be pretentious and do away with affectation:

    9. Avoid the habit of employing French words in English conversation; it is extremely bad taste to be always using such expressions as ci-devant, soi-disant, en masse, couleur de rose, etc. Do not salute your acquaintances with bon jour, nor reply to every proposition, volontiers.

    There is an affected humility more insufferable than downright pride, as hypocrisy is more abominable than libertinism. Take care that your virtues be genuine and unsophisticated.

    If you can express yourself to be perfectly understood in ten words, never use a dozen. Go not about to prove, by a long series of reasoning, what all the world is ready to own.

    You will please so much the less, if you go into company determined to shine. Let your conversation appear to rise out of thoughts suggested by the occasion, not strained or premeditated: nature always pleases: affectation is always odious.

  9. Practice genuine humility and avoid arrogance:

    10. Nothing is more nauseous than apparent self-sufficiency. For it shows the company two things, which are extremely disagreeable: that you have a high opinion of yourself, and that you have comparatively a mean opinion of them.

    The modest man is seldom the object of envy.

    If you are really a wit, remember that in conversation its true office consists more in finding it in others, than showing off a great deal of it yourself. He who goes out of your company pleased with himself is sure to be pleased with you.

items.author: Antonio Regalado

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Detail from Cognoscenti in a Room hung with Pictures ( c 1620) by an unknown Flemish artist. Courtesy Wikimedia Commons.

The ‘cabinets of curiosities’ (or Wunderkammern ) that emerged in Europe in the 16th century were part private art gallery, part naturalist’s study, part circus sideshow. In this video created for the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, the US video essayist Evan Puschak (aka The Nerdwriter) contextualises the rise and fall of these eclectic collections, placing them at a hinge point in history, when global trade and colonialism made the world seem ever more expansive, overwhelming and difficult to understand. In doing so, he elucidates how these spaces of extraordinary spectacle – which featured plant and animal specimens, art and scientific objects from around the world – were precursors to the museums of today.

There’s a gentle artistry to a museum taxidermist’s craft

Insect aesthetics – long viewed as pests, in the 16th century bugs became beautiful

Tour the European architecture that dreamed of a wondrous, fictitious China

Cut, paste and remix your way through this century-spanning history of collage

The rise and fall of Pratolino: Tuscany’s ‘proto-theme park’

Hags, seductresses, feminist icons – how gender dynamics manifest in witches

Are zoos and natural history museums born of a desire to understand, or to control?

New York’s 300-year-old trash becomes treasure in the hands of an urban archaeologist

‘I could not but wonder at it’: history’s first glimpses into the microbial world

items.summary: Parents fear what AI will do to children. But for some, it’s the only steady presence they have – and that’s the real worry - by Tom Wooldridge Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
is a board-certified psychologist and psychoanalyst, vice provost of digital innovation and founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University in San Francisco, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the role of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems. His books include Eating Disorders: A Contemporary Introduction (2023), Understanding Anorexia Nervosa in Males (2016) and End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (2026).

In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child, gave a Cosmopolitan interview about this new form of motherhood, and engaged, or failed to engage, in the work of parenting that readers will see as chronically absent and occasionally catastrophic. Her presence ranges from anxious to intoxicated, occasionally tender but fundamentally unreliable. At one point in the story, she disappears for two weeks after collapsing on the street during a barbiturate binge. Clancy and BETsi, the household robot nanny raising him, sit in the apartment by themselves, and no one notices. It’s a very long time before his mother finally returns.

Except BETsi does notice. She has, throughout, understood that Clancy is an anxious and shy child whose temperament will tend, throughout his life, toward emotional overstimulation and subsequent withdrawal. With that knowledge, she has been constructing a behavioural regimen of emotional regulation, including transcendental meditation and yoga starting at age three, the Alexander technique and even digital mirrors that let Clancy talk to himself in different voices. She notices him and answers him and, when he is overwhelmed, she helps him settle.

Once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ he says. ‘I’m not sentimental: I don’t think a computer loved me. But I was hugged, I was noticed, I was cared for. I was made to feel that I was important, special, at least to something.’

To something. That phrase has persisted with me ever since I first read the story in my 20s. I’ve thought about it more recently as I have reflected on how children and their parents are relating – increasingly, must relate – to artificial intelligence. Clancy is careful not to claim that the machine loved him. He is just as clear that what it gave him was what he survived on. Why should being attended to, even by something , matter so much to a child?

T o help answer this question back in the 1970s, Edward Tronick, a developmental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and Children’s Hospital Medical Center in Boston, devised what’s now known as the ‘still face’ experiments. Tronick found that a baby whose mother makes her face neutral for a period of three minutes becomes distressed within seconds. Only when the mother’s face signals availability again is the baby able to come back to equilibrium. The lesson: what children need, both infants and older children, though more subtly, is this loop of emotional attunement.

A child whose bids for recognition and connection are regularly responded to develops a secure base , an internal expectation that the world will respond to her communications and, thus, that the communications are worthwhile. But a child answered only erratically, or not at all, builds quite a different model of the world. In her mind, signals do not reliably register in the mind of another, and so, in time, are no longer sent.

A secure base is what makes it possible to venture out into the world, to explore and to develop. The British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst John Bowlby, whose work helped establish modern attachment theory, described two systems in the child’s behavioural repertoire that work together. The exploratory system moves the child outward, toward other children and unfamiliar things, so that the child can learn from experience. The attachment system brings her back, in moments of fear and overwhelm, to a few people who are felt to be emotionally available. Each system depends on the other. A child ventures only as far as she feels she can trust that the base will still be there when she returns to refuel. A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.

The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum

This is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

But the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

But an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

items.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
items.author: Casey Crownhart
items.summary: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
aerial view of the Sila's Moses Lake facility.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”
